Sharp Credit Freeze Hits Ghana’s Electric Utilities, Leaving Sector in Turmoil

A sudden freeze in credit markets has plunged Ghana’s electric utilities sector into a deepening financial crisis, with several major operators teetering on the brink of insolvency and widespread project delays disrupting service delivery across the country.

The crisis began last week, when lenders abruptly tightened access to short-term financing for power providers, following concerns over mounting unpaid bills and government arrears. As a result, companies such as Volta Electric, Akosombo Power, and Unity Grid have reported being unable to secure the working capital needed to maintain operations or invest in urgent infrastructure repairs.

At a press briefing in Accra on Tuesday, Samuel K. Boateng, president of the Ghana Utilities Association, said, “We are facing a liquidity crunch unprecedented in our industry’s history. Lines of credit that sustained our daily operations have evaporated almost overnight. Without immediate intervention, reliable electricity supply is at serious risk.”

The Electricity Workers Union has warned that delayed salaries and suspension of overtime payments are already affecting staff morale and raising the prospect of industrial action. “Our members are worried about their jobs, their families, and their ability to keep the lights on for Ghanaians,” said union secretary Agnes Mensah. “We urge all stakeholders to act swiftly before the situation deteriorates further.”

The impact has been felt most acutely in projects aimed at grid expansion and maintenance. According to the Ghana Power Regulatory Service, at least twelve planned upgrades in the Northern and Western regions have been put on hold, while routine repairs are being scaled back to conserve cash. “Deferred maintenance means increased risk of outages, especially as we approach the rainy season,” said regulatory spokesperson Kwame Adusei.

Industry analysts estimate that sector-wide debts now exceed GHS 3.7 billion, with outstanding payments to suppliers and contractors mounting daily. “The immediate concern is whether utilities can avoid defaulting on key obligations, including fuel purchases for thermal plants,” said Anita Owusu, an energy sector analyst in Kumasi.

The Ministry of Energy has pledged to convene crisis talks this week with banks and utility leaders, but has so far announced no concrete measures. “We are monitoring developments closely and are committed to restoring stability in the electricity sector,” a ministry statement read.

As the credit freeze continues, utility heads have appealed for urgent government guarantees and emergency financing to keep power flowing and stave off deeper disruption.
